extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of social/economic theory (sociology, political economy)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the conceptual standards and canons Veblen uses to evaluate social behavior, consumption, and the standard of living in The Theory of the Leisure Class. Focuses on criteria such as conspicuous consumption, leisure, workmanship instinct, reputability, habit formation, and related social forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous consumption as evidence of pecuniary repute
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumption whose primary function is to demonstrate pecuniary strength and to impress transient or social observers; the signature of one's pecuniary strength should be 'written in characters which he who runs may read.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most serviceable where human contact is wide and population mobility is great (urban settings). It heightens with urbanization and attendance at large gatherings; it becomes a prescriptive standard of decency and compels higher expenditure to indicate a given degree of pecuniary decency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous leisure as honorific evidence of wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Leisure that functions as an exponent of wealth and stands as evidence of exemption from ignoble labor; initially more prominent as a basis of reputability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leisure was ascendant in early (quasi-peaceable) stages where noble/ignoble employment distinctions prevailed. Its social value lies in showing exemption from productive labor; it later yields relatively to consumption but remains an important form of reputability (including vicarious leisure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon of reputability / standard of decency
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of social rules and conventions that determine what expenditures and behaviors are considered decent or honorific within a class; flexible and extensible rather than rigid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set in large outline by the leisure (upper) class and transmitted downward; changes slowly, constrained by economic circumstances, traditions, and the instinct of workmanship. Its main effect is to prevent recession from an established scale of conspicuous expenditure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinct of workmanship as countervailing standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An instinctive disposition favoring productive efficiency, usefulness, and aversion to obvious waste; acts as an auxiliary canon of self-complacency that tempers conspicuous waste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operates more strongly as societies move from slave to wage-labor regimes (peaceable industry); it condemns obviously futile expenditures and seeks some ostensible purpose even in wasteful outlay. Its judgments appeal to impersonal usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical definition of 'conspicuous waste'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Waste' means expenditure incurred on the ground of an invidious pecuniary comparison — spending that does not serve human life or well-being on the whole but is chosen for reputability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term is technical and not meant as moral censure in economic theory: an expenditure is 'waste' if its primary ground is invidious pecuniary comparison. The test of wastefulness (for the instinct of workmanship) is whether the expenditure furthers human life impersonally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of impersonal usefulness (criterion for waste vs use)
rubrics_metrics.description: To decide whether an expenditure is 'waste' bring it to the test of whether it serves or furthers human life on the whole — usefulness viewed impersonally, not merely the consumer's private gratification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customary expenditure counts as waste if traceable to invidious pecuniary comparison. Items can have both useful and wasteful elements; the net effect on general human well-being is the measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit formation and persistence of standards of living
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards of living are habitual scales of response; once a scale of conspicuous expenditure is established it is hard to recede from and easier to advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retrogression is morally and practically difficult; increases in capacity to pay typically result in increased conspicuous consumption. The longer and more ingrained the habit, and the more it coincides with inherited aptitudes, the more persistent it is under countervailing circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emulation (propensity for invidious comparison) as primary motive
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency to compare with and emulate those just above one in social rank drives conspicuous consumption; it is one of the strongest economic motives after self-preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards of decency are set by the class immediately above; emulation absorbs increases in industrial efficiency into conspicuous waste rather than easing strain. Emulation is indefinitely expansible and readily reasserts itself when new means become available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of population mobility and urban environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Urbanization and high mobility increase the serviceability of conspicuous consumption as a means of repute, because acquaintances are transient and observers numerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Urban populations, because of wider human contact and mobility, habitually allocate more income to conspicuous consumption and live more 'hand-to-mouth' to maintain appearance compared with rural populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicarious leisure and domestic conspicuousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of leisure displayed vicariously (e.g., household decoration, ceremonial domestic observances) serve as honorific consumption — the housewife's assiduous household cares become a visible sign of leisure and status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vicarious leisure adapts to the instinct of workmanship by turning to ostensible productive or ceremonial activities; such activities are often intertwined with genuine purposeful effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-believe purposeful activity as reconciliation
rubrics_metrics.description: To reconcile the disdain for productive effort with the instinct of workmanship, elites adopt 'make-believe' purposes — social duties, organizations, ceremonies — that appear purposeful but primarily serve reputability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These observances provide ostensible justification for activity while preserving the honorific character of leisure; often they contain some element of genuine purposeful effort mixed with ceremonialism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative tenacity of different consumption habits (necessaries vs higher wants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different habitual expenditures have varying persistence: necessaries (subsistence minimum) are given up last, while higher wants and honorific expenditures vary in tenacity depending on habituation and inherited aptitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some higher wants (e.g., habitual stimulants, religious observances, good repute) may in certain individuals take precedence over lower wants. Persistence depends on length of habituation and congruence with temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Savings/home comforts as alternative signals in rural settings
rubrics_metrics.description: In rural populations, savings and home comforts — known through neighborhood gossip — serve as effective means of pecuniary repute, partly substituting for conspicuous consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because everyone's affairs are more visible in small communities, savings and domestic comforts advertise pecuniary status more effectively than ostentatious consumption does in that environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity: useful goods contain waste element and vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: Few items are purely wasteful or purely useful; consumable and productive goods typically combine elements of use and waste in varying proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification requires examining origins in invidious comparison and net effect on human well-being; even ostentatious objects often have ostensible useful purposes, and useful goods may carry traces of ostentation.
